title: What are the most common case interview mistakes, and how do you avoid them?
description: The mistakes almost everyone makes in case interviews, grouped by when they happen, with what to do instead.
hook: The most common case interview mistakes are predictable: a generic structure with no hypothesis, waiting to be told what to do, describing charts instead of drawing insights, silent maths that nobody checks, and a recommendation that replays the whole case. Because they are predictable, each one has a simple fix you can practise. Here they are in the order they happen, with what to say instead.
body:
In this guide

  • Why the same mistakes keep happening
  • Mistakes in the first five minutes
  • Mistakes in the middle of the case
  • Mistakes at the end
  • Mistakes all the way through
  • How to recover when you get something wrong
  • Traps that belong to a case type
  • Mistakes in how you prepare
  • Check yourself

Why the same mistakes keep happening

A case asks you to think, calculate and talk at the same time, in front of a stranger who is judging you. Under that load, almost everyone falls back on the same habits: buying time, describing instead of concluding, and waiting for permission. Making these mistakes in practice is not a sign you are bad at cases. It is what practice is for. The aim is to make each fix automatic before the real interview.

Mistakes in the first five minutes

Nodding along without writing down the goal

You hear the prompt, feel you understand it and start structuring. Ten minutes later you realise you do not know whether the client wants more profit, more market share or a yes-or-no decision. Fix: write the objective at the top of your page, in the client's words, and check it in your recap. See what to do while the case is read to you.

Reading the prompt back word for word

A recap is not a transcript. Fix: say it in one or two sentences, with the numbers and the goal.

Weak: "So the client is a company that makes bikes and they've been in business for 20 years and they sell in Germany and France and their profits have gone down..."
Strong: "A bike maker selling in Germany and France, profit down 20% in two years, and we need to find out why and fix it. Is that right?"

Asking a long list of clarifying questions

Seven questions in a row looks like stalling. Fix: ask three at most, and only ones whose answers would change your structure: the goal, the timeframe, and whether the problem is the client's alone or the whole market's.

A generic structure with no hypothesis

"Internal factors and external factors" fits every company on earth, which is why it impresses nobody. Fix: build buckets from this client's business and say where you would start, and why. How to present your structure shows the difference.

Mistakes in the middle of the case

Ending every answer with "where would you like me to go next?"

That hands the steering wheel back. In a candidate-led case it is the single most common way to lose points. Fix: end every answer with a proposal: "Next I'd like to look at costs by store, because that is where the gap is." The interviewer will redirect you if they want something else, and you still get credit for leading.

Describing a chart instead of reading it

Weak: "This shows revenue for the four regions over three years. The North is blue."
Strong: "Three regions are growing about 5% a year; the North has fallen by a third. That is our problem. Do we know what changed there?"

Fix: read the title, axes and units in your head, then say the one thing that matters and what it means for the goal.

Silent maths, and no sanity check

Thirty seconds of silence followed by a wrong number is the worst combination. Fix: state your approach before you calculate ("Revenue is customers times average spend, so 40,000 times $25"), say each step, write units next to every number, and check the result against something you know. If a corner shop comes out at $40M a year, something has gone wrong.

Brainstorming a random list

Ten ideas in the order they came to mind sound like panic. Fix: two or three buckets first (for example, "raise prices, sell more, cut costs"), then ideas inside each, then say which you would pursue first.

Mistakes at the end

Replaying the whole case

"So first we looked at revenue, then we looked at costs..." The interviewer was there. Fix: answer first, then reasons. The 60-second recommendation gives you the template.

Weak: "So, I think there are a few things the client could consider..."
Strong: "The client should close the two loss-making stores. They lose $1.2M a year between them, and closing them recovers most of the profit drop. The risk is losing loyal customers to competitors, so I'd move them to the nearest store with a loyalty offer. Next step: check the leases for break clauses."

Hedging

"It depends" is not a recommendation. Fix: commit to an answer on the evidence you have, then name what would change your mind.

Mistakes all the way through

  • Losing the link to the goal. Every few minutes, say how the latest finding moves you towards the client's objective.
  • Letting nerves run the show. Speaking faster and faster, apologising, filling silence. A short pause to think is fine; say "Let me take 30 seconds to structure this." Staying calm when nerves hit has the techniques.
  • Ignoring hints. When an interviewer asks "Are you sure?" or "What about the other region?", they are helping. Stop and look again.
  • Defending an answer you know is wrong. See the next section.

How to recover when you get something wrong

Interviewers expect mistakes. What they score is how you handle them. Suppose you are working out a client's market share. Client sales are $60M and you divide by the $200M market and say 30%. Then you notice the $200M was last year's figure; this year the market is $240M.

"I used the wrong denominator. With this year's $240M market, our share is $60M ÷ $240M = 25%, not 30%. That changes the story: the market grew 20% and we stood still, so we are losing share rather than holding it."

Three things happened there: you named the error plainly, you corrected it, and you said whether the conclusion changes. That is quicker and more impressive than burying the mistake under more analysis. The same applies to a hypothesis the data has disproved: drop it out loud and move to the next branch.

Traps that belong to a case type

Each kind of case has its own classic mistake. The case types page covers all seventeen; these are the ones that catch people most.

Case typeThe trapDo this instead
ProfitabilityDiagnosing before segmentingSplit revenue and costs by product, region or channel first
Revenue dropTreating revenue as one numberBreak it into volume × price, then by segment
Market entryForgetting how to enterCover build, partner or buy, plus timing and a pilot
GrowthA list of ideas with no sizesSize each idea roughly and rank them
M&AIgnoring integration and the do-nothing optionCompare the deal with not doing it
PricingUsing one lens and no volume assumptionCheck cost, competitor and value, and model volume
Cost cuttingCutting costs that carry revenueAsk what each cost buys before cutting it
ValuationAdding future years without discountingDiscount cash flows, or use a sensible multiple
Public sectorForcing a profit lens onto a social goalAgree the success measure first

Mistakes in how you prepare

  • Doing case after case without reviewing. Five cases with the same error teach you the error. After each one, write down a single fix.
  • Writing vague fixes. "Be more careful" changes nothing. "Write units above every division" does.
  • Only practising the middle. Rehearse openings and closes on their own; they are short and easy to repeat.
  • Never practising out loud. Silent practice hides the problems that show up when you speak.

Check yourself

1. You finish a calculation and the interviewer says nothing. What do you say?

Show the answer

The so-what and a next step: "So the new line would add $3M of profit a year, which covers the gap. Next I'd check whether we have the capacity to make it." Never leave a number hanging.

2. Rewrite this close: "There are a few options, and it depends on the client's priorities."

Show the answer

Lead with a decision and a number: "The client should do X, because it adds $Y. The main risk is Z, so the next step is to test it with a pilot." If you are genuinely unsure, still commit, and say what evidence would change your view.

3. A client's revenue is $45M in a $300M market. You said their share is 20%. Is that right?

Show the answer

No. $45M ÷ $300M = 15%. Say so plainly, correct it and check whether your conclusion still holds.

Where to go next

Pick the one mistake from this list you make most and spend a week on it. What to say at each stage gives you replacement phrases, and practising on your own shows how to drill a single fix in short sessions.
